title: Daily Standup: Stop Reporting, Start Walking the Board
summary: A study of daily standups found 'what I did yesterday' took the most time of the three questions and rarely led anywhere. Try a board walk that shows what's stuck.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
9:30, the video call opens and the usual round begins. One person reads out yesterday. The next one reads from the board. Someone says "no blockers" while their face says otherwise. The meeting ends on time, which feels efficient, but nothing has changed. Everyone reported status, and the day isn't any clearer than before.

The standup is so familiar that teams stop asking what it's for. It slides into a roll call: what I did, what I'll do, am I blocked. That format is easy to perform. People learn how to sound busy, the board doesn't change, and the team learns very little. This post is about one switch that fixes most of it: stop going through people and start going through the work.

What researchers saw in 102 standups

Viktoria Stray, Nils Brede Moe and Dag Sjøberg spent years studying this one meeting. They observed 102 daily standups and interviewed 60 people in 15 teams across five countries (Daily Stand-Up Meetings: Start Breaking the Rules, IEEE Software). When they transcribed and coded eight of those meetings, only about a third of the time (34%) went to the classic three questions. Almost as much (31%) went to what they call problem-focused communication: digging into a problem, discussing fixes and making decisions. In interviews, that problem-solving was the benefit people mentioned most often.

The status part looked very different. Within the three questions, "what did I do yesterday" took about two thirds of the time, even though it was the question people least wanted to spend time on, and it rarely started a useful discussion. Today's plan or a fresh obstacle did. The researchers also spotted what turns a standup into a status meeting: when the facilitator got people talking to them, updates flowed to one person and the team stopped talking to each other. One participant said it felt like having oral exams every day.

The rulebook already moved on

If your team runs "yesterday, today, blockers" because Scrum seems to require it, good news: it doesn't. The Scrum Guide describes the Daily Scrum as a 15-minute event for the Developers to "inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary", and says they "can select whatever structure and techniques they want." The 2020 revision removed the Daily Scrum questions altogether (Scrum Guide revision history). The three questions live on as habit, and you're free to drop them.

Walk the board, right to left

Jason Yip's catalog of standup patterns has the simplest fix: walk the board. Go through each work item on your board, starting at the end of the process and moving back toward the start (It's Not Just Standing Up). He describes it as a meeting where the work items attend and people speak for them. For each card, ask:

  • What's closest to done, and what does it need to get there today?
  • What's sitting in review or QA, and who can pick it up?
  • What's waiting on an answer from someone outside the team?
  • What's been in progress longer than it should be?

This changes the mood of the meeting. Nobody has to justify their yesterday. The question on the table becomes "how do we help this card move?", and the person holding it gets help instead of scrutiny. A board walk also shows things a round of updates hides: three cards waiting on the same reviewer, or a card nobody has touched in four days because its owner got pulled into an incident.

Make small blockers easy to say

Most blockers aren't dramatic. They're small doubts: an API contract nobody has confirmed, a test environment acting strange, a reviewer who's swamped, a product edge case nobody wants to decide. If "blocker" only means "I can't do anything", people keep these to themselves. By the time someone officially says they're blocked, two days are gone.

Walking the board helps here because the card speaks first. "This one has been in review since Monday" is a fact, not a confession. When the conversation is about the card, it's much easier to say "the payment callback still isn't confirmed and I'm not sure who owns it." Leads can help by thanking people who raise half-formed risks, especially the first few times.

Finish before you start

If the team opens five new tasks while three old ones are nearly done, it's creating motion without finishing anything. A board walk shows that in the first two minutes, because the nearly-done items come up first. A good standup asks: what can we finish today before we pick up anything new? Who needs a hand to close something out? Which interesting item should wait until tomorrow? Choosing the order of the day is the strategy part of the meeting. If your board keeps filling up in the middle, Kanban or Scrum? goes deeper on WIP limits.

What the facilitator should do

Leads and managers need a light touch here. If every update gets a verdict, the standup turns into a stage. If every blocker becomes a 20-minute fix-it session, the meeting gets heavy and people start editing what they say. A healthy pattern: name the issue, agree who'll pick up the conversation afterwards, and move on. Yip calls this "Take It Offline". The standup opens doors. It doesn't have to walk through every one of them.

Stray and her colleagues add two recommendations. First, team members should talk to each other. When everyone faces the facilitator, you get the smell Yip calls "Reporting to the Leader". Second, share the facilitation by rotating who runs the meeting. When the facilitator isn't also the team lead, the standup is less likely to slide into status reporting. It was the recommendation teams adopted least in their study, probably because Scrum Masters and leads see running the meeting as their job. It's still worth a try for one Sprint.

Timing, frequency and remote teams

The same study questions two habits most teams never think about. Morning standups often broke up the day: some people put off hard work before the meeting because they knew they'd be interrupted. Many teams that moved the meeting to right before lunch liked it, since it folds two interruptions into one. The researchers also suggest that a team that already talks a lot may not need to meet every day; three or four times a week can be enough. Status itself can live somewhere else, on the board or in a short async note collected in chat.

For distributed teams, they found that facilitators who used video, and not only audio, ran more discussion-style meetings, because people could see whether others were following. Whatever format you choose, the team needs some daily way to look at the flow of work and adjust. The ceremony is negotiable. The feedback loop isn't.

The one-question check

After standup, ask yourself: what did this meeting change? Who's pairing with whom, which PR gets reviewed first, which risk gets escalated, what waits until tomorrow. If the honest answer is "nothing" several days in a row, the team is reporting and not coordinating. Turning a board walk into clear calls is the next step, and The Daily Standup That Changes Decisions picks up from there.

Try this week

  • Run one standup as a board walk, right to left, with no round of names.
  • Drop "what did you do yesterday?" for a week and see whether anyone misses it.
  • Hand the facilitator role to someone else for the next Sprint.
  • Try a slot right before lunch for a week.
  • End each standup by saying out loud one thing that changed.

faqs.q: What should a daily standup cover?
faqs.a: Progress toward the team's goal and what to adjust for the next day. A practical format is to walk the board from right to left: what's closest to done, what's stuck in review or QA, what's waiting on someone outside the team and what has been open too long. Raise problems, agree who follows up afterwards, and keep detailed problem-solving out of the main meeting.

faqs.q: Do we still have to use the three standup questions?
faqs.a: No. The 2020 Scrum Guide removed the Daily Scrum questions and lets Developers choose any structure that focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal. Research by Stray, Moe and Sjøberg found that 'what did I do yesterday' took the most time while rarely leading to useful discussion, and they recommend dropping it.

faqs.q: How long should a daily standup be?
faqs.a: The Scrum Guide sets the Daily Scrum at 15 minutes. If it keeps running over, the usual cause is problem-solving inside the meeting. Name the issue, agree who will discuss it right after, and move on to the next item on the board.

faqs.q: Does every team need a standup every day?
faqs.a: Not always. Stray and colleagues suggest that teams that already communicate well may only need to meet three or four times a week, and that status can be shared on the board or through short async notes. Whatever the format, the team still needs a daily way to look at the flow of work and adjust.
